lesson.title: Reading an Ionic Formula Out Loud, Correctly
lesson.summary: Naming ionic compounds follows a small set of consistent rules: name the cation first, then the anion, and use a Roman numeral whenever the metal's charge is not fixed.
lesson.body:
Every ionic compound name follows the same basic order: cation first, then anion, with nothing in between. If the cation is a metal that forms only one possible charge, like the group 1 and group 2 metals, its name is simply the element name, unchanged. If the anion is a single element, its name is built by taking the root of the element's name and adding the suffix -ide, so chlorine becomes chloride, oxygen becomes oxide, and nitrogen becomes nitride. Sodium chloride is therefore just sodium plus chloride, and magnesium oxide is magnesium plus oxide, no extra information needed because Na is always 1+ and Mg is always 2+.

Polyatomic ions keep their own names unchanged in a compound's name, they are never converted to an -ide ending, since that ending is reserved for single-element anions. Calcium carbonate is calcium plus carbonate, not calcium carbide, which is actually a completely different compound, CaC2, containing the carbide ion. Magnesium sulfate is magnesium plus sulfate. Getting comfortable with the list of common polyatomic ion names from the previous section is what makes this step reliable rather than guesswork.

The complication arrives with metals, mostly the transition metals, that can form more than one stable cation. Iron, for instance, commonly forms both Fe2+ and Fe3+, and copper commonly forms both Cu+ and Cu2+. Simply saying iron chloride would leave the charge, and therefore the actual formula, ambiguous, since FeCl2 and FeCl3 are two different compounds with different properties. Chemists solve this with the Stock system, inserting a Roman numeral in parentheses immediately after the metal name to state its charge in that specific compound. FeCl2 is named iron(II) chloride, because two 1- chloride ions balance a 2+ iron ion. FeCl3 is named iron(III) chloride, because three 1- chloride ions require a 3+ iron ion. Cu2O is copper(I) oxide, since two Cu+ ions balance one O2- ion, while CuO is copper(II) oxide, since one Cu2+ ion balances one O2- ion directly.

Working out the Roman numeral is a small charge-balancing calculation, not a memorized fact. Take Fe2O3: oxide is always 2-, and there are three oxide ions present, contributing a total negative charge of 6-. For the compound to be electrically neutral, the two iron ions together must contribute 6+, so each individual iron ion must be 3+, giving the name iron(III) oxide, the compound better known as rust. This same logic, total negative charge from the anions divided among the cations present, works for any variable-charge metal paired with any anion, monatomic or polyatomic.

An older naming system, still occasionally seen on reagent bottles and in older textbooks, uses -ous and -ic suffixes on the Latin root of the metal name instead of Roman numerals, with -ous marking the lower charge and -ic marking the higher one. In that system, Fe2+ is ferrous and Fe3+ is ferric, so FeCl2 is ferrous chloride and FeCl3 is ferric chloride. The Roman numeral system is unambiguous and is what modern chemistry uses by default, but recognizing the older names is still useful for reading historical or industrial sources.
